slot.brief: Cylindrical/spherical charge distribution with charge density varying linearly with radius shown in figure; use Gauss's law to find field at a point inside the distribution.

stem: A solid insulating sphere of radius $R$ has volume charge density $\rho(s)=\rho_0(1-s/R)$, where $s$ is distance from its centre and $\rho_0>0$. As shown in the figure, what is the electric field magnitude at $P$?

verdicts.working: By spherical symmetry, Gauss’s law gives E(r)=ρ₀/ε₀(r/3−r²/(4R)). From the figure, P is at r=R/2, so E=5ρ₀R/(48ε₀).

working:
$q_{\text{enc}}=4\pi\rho_0\int_0^{R/2}(1-s/R)s^2\,ds=\dfrac{5\pi\rho_0R^3}{48}$; $E( R/2)=\dfrac{q_{\text{enc}}}{4\pi\varepsilon_0(R/2)^2}=\dfrac{5\rho_0R}{48\varepsilon_0}$.

Independent check: By spherical symmetry, Gauss’s law gives E(r)=ρ₀/ε₀(r/3−r²/(4R)). From the figure, P is at r=R/2, so E=5ρ₀R/(48ε₀).

figure.description: Draw a circle as a cross-section of the sphere, with centre O and boundary. Draw a horizontal radius from O to the right-hand boundary, label its full length R, and mark P halfway along it with OP=R/2. Add a callout stating that the volume charge density at radial distance s from O is ρ(s)=ρ₀(1−s/R).

draft.distractor_notes: A: treats the density at P as uniform throughout the enclosed sphere. C: uses an incorrect radial weighting when averaging the density over the enclosed volume. D: treats the density as its central value throughout the enclosed sphere.
